Our $K_{\text{eff}}$ framework and process-$\kappa$ metric generalize to any trace aggregation method; the confirmation bias mechanism applies to any self-verification pipeline. A cross-architecture proof-of-concept (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}) shows the gap is recoverable when verification comes from an independent model.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch: same-model traces carry correlated errors, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct shared bias.

Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions alleviate this, but the core limitation persists.
Recent neuro-symbolic methods \citep{pan2023logiclm, olausson2023linc, xu2026dylos, li2025aristotle, wang2025fover, luo2025logicagent} report gains on logical reasoning but introduce components beyond the reasoning model.
A simpler question precedes these: can the \emph{same} model extract useful formal constraints from its own traces---a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model or data?
No prior work has systematically evaluated this.

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.

We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 condition-evaluations (${\sim}$1,250 unique instances) with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Twenty-plus remediation strategies spanning fifteen families---from prompt engineering through method-level redesign---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is persistent at the 7B--32B scale.

Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: same-model gold FOL yields $+29.90$\,pp (Mistral-7B) and $+14.22$\,pp (Qwen-14B) on FOLIO ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only ${\sim}$12\% of the same-model ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
The central finding is a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
A cross-architecture proof-of-concept shows that this gap is recoverable: DeBERTa-large NLI combined with SC achieves $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.039$, McNemar exact test) through per-label complementarity (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off and Cross-Architecture Escape.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a same-model trade-off ceiling ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). Twenty-plus remediation strategies spanning fifteen families fail; a cross-architecture NLI verifier (DeBERTa-large, $+3.43$\,pp, $p = 0.039$) shows the ceiling is escapable (\S\ref{sec:remediation}, \S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} On incorrect problems, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence.} Across four model families, CoT cosine similarity ($0.69$--$0.79$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.45$--$0.74$); the gap intensifies with model capability, showing reasoning homogeneity is architecture-independent (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
\end{enumerate}

2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	This section investigates \emph{why} SICA fails: trace correlation (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}), symbolic confirmation bias (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}), process-level independence (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}), supporting diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:diagnostics}), and remediation strategies (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

6	\subsection{Condorcet Effective-K}
7	\label{sec:effective-k}

Two conditions are jointly necessary for positive $\Delta$: sufficient $K_{\text{eff}}$ ($\leq 1.30$ never improves) and sufficient SC accuracy ($K_{\text{eff}} = 3.62$ with SC $= 39\%$ produces significant degradation). 41	\subsection{Symbolic Confirmation Bias}
42	\label{sec:confirmation-bias}
43	
44	The trace correlation above manifests through a specific mechanism that explains \emph{all three} regime failures: self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer regardless of correctness. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), when SICA errs, 83.3\% of extracted constraints support the incorrect majority answer---a bias ratio of $4.97\times$ (raw constraint counts; $4.24\times$ when MaxSAT-weighted) compared to correct problems. Consequently, 94\% of SICA errors overlap with SC errors: symbolic aggregation adds no independent corrective signal.
45	
46	The causal chain is: the model generates an answer, then extracts FOL consistent with it. Constraints from majority-answer traces use trace-specific variable names (56.4\% of cross-answer pairs share zero Z3 variables; Z3 operates over logical structure via alpha-equivalence, mitigating this syntactic confound), so MAX-SAT retains nearly all, and aggregation reduces to a weighted majority vote (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}). Confirmation bias generalizes across model families: bias ratios of $4.97\times$ (Mistral-7B), $3.93\times$ (Qwen2.5-14B), and $2.88\times$ (LLaMA-3.1-8B) all significantly exceed $1.0$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model-bias}). The bias ratio gradient aligns with regime boundaries: high bias (Mistral, $4.24\times$ weighted) at intermediate SC produces SICA's only positive trends; low bias (LLaMA, $2.66\times$) at high SC produces the worst degradation ($-4.41$\,pp), because low confirmation bias at high SC means the model's consensus is already near-correct and constraints provide no leverage. The oracle ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) confirms that ${\sim}$88\% of the same-model potential gain is lost to self-extraction quality.
47	
48	
49	\subsection{Process-Level Independence}
50	\label{sec:process-kappa}
51	
52	Answer-level $\kappa$ may underestimate the independence bottleneck: two traces can follow nearly identical reasoning yet reach different final answers, causing $\kappa$ to treat them as disagreeing. We define process similarity as the mean pairwise cosine similarity of TF-IDF trace representations:
53	\begin{equation}
54	\label{eq:process-sim}
55	\text{ProcessSim}(q) = \frac{2}{K(K{-}1)} \sum_{i < j} \cos(\mathbf{v}_i^q, \mathbf{v}_j^q),
56	\end{equation}
57	where $\mathbf{v}_i^q$ is the TF-IDF vector of trace $t_i$ for question $q$. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), mean ProcessSim is $0.69$, far exceeding answer-level $\kappa = 0.41$. The process--answer correlation is model-strength dependent: $r = -0.06$ ($p = 0.36$) on Mistral-7B, where answer diversity does not reflect reasoning diversity (Figure~\ref{fig:process-kappa}), rising to $r = +0.24$ ($p < 0.001$) on Qwen2.5-14B. This pattern generalizes across four families (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model-process}): the cosine--$\kappa$ gap narrows from $0.23$ (Mistral) to $0.02$ (Qwen-14B), meaning answer-level $\kappa$ already captures the bottleneck for strong models, while process-$\kappa$ reveals hidden homogeneity in weaker models where answer diversity masks process convergence. In all families, interventions targeting answer diversity (temperature scaling, diverse prompting) cannot alter the underlying reasoning paths. TF-IDF cosine similarity captures lexical overlap rather than semantic equivalence, making it a lower bound on true process similarity; semantic embedding methods would likely yield even higher values.

65	\end{figure}

68	\label{sec:diagnostics}
69

73	\subsection{Remediation Analysis}
74	\label{sec:remediation}
75	\label{sec:interventions}
76	
77	We test more than twenty remediation strategies spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions. All produce neutral or negative results.
78	
79	\paragraph{Prompt-level interventions.} Nine strategies spanning six dimensions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:remediation}) all fail: contrastive prompting reduces non-discriminative constraints but $\Delta = -1.1$\,pp; cross-model extraction yields accuracy within $\pm 1$\,pp; multi-temperature ($T \in \{0.3, 0.7, 1.2\}$) yields $\Delta = 0.00$\,pp.
80	
81	\paragraph{Method-level interventions.} ICG ($\Delta \approx 0$, $p = .206$), Contrastive ($\Delta = -9.31$\,pp, $p < 0.01$), and Debate ($\Delta = -18.63$/$-23.00$\,pp, $p < 0.001$) all fail; three of six conditions reach significance, all negative (Table~\ref{tab:method_interventions}, Appendix~\ref{app:remediation}).
82	
83	\paragraph{Additional directions.} Ten further experiments---code verification, iterative refinement, logprob filtering, cross-model ensembles, alternative objectives---all produce neutral-to-negative results (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:additional_interventions}).
84

+\subsection{The Symbolic Mirage Hypothesis}
+\label{sec:mirage}

+The CJT framework (\S\ref{sec:condorcet}) identifies \emph{when} self-consistency fails (correlated voters); the SICA pipeline (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}) provides a concrete mechanism for leveraging symbolic constraints. We now introduce a unifying hypothesis that predicts \emph{why} self-extracted constraints cannot serve as independent verification.
+\paragraph{Definition.}

+We define the \textbf{Symbolic Mirage}: self-extracted symbolic structures from an LLM are not independent verification signals but high-dimensional projections of the model's own distributional biases. Under this hypothesis, any same-model symbolic verification---regardless of prompting strategy, scoring function, or aggregation mechanism---is contaminated by the generating model's answer distribution.

+Formally, let $f_\theta$ denote a model with parameters $\theta$, and let $\mathcal{E}_\theta(t_i)$ denote the FOL constraints extracted by $f_\theta$ from its own trace $t_i$ with answer $a_i$. The Symbolic Mirage hypothesis states:
+\begin{equation}
+\label{eq:mirage}
+P\bigl(\mathcal{E}_\theta(t_i) \mid a^*, a_i\bigr) \neq P\bigl(\mathcal{E}_\theta(t_i) \mid a^*\bigr),
+\end{equation}

+i.e., extracted constraints are not conditionally independent of the model's answer $a_i$ given the ground truth $a^*$. When $a_i \neq a^*$, this dependence causes constraints to systematically support the wrong answer.
+\paragraph{Predicted consequences.}

+The mirage degrades constraint-based aggregation through two channels. The \emph{direct} channel: correlated traces produce correlated constraints, compressing effective diversity to $K_{\text{eff}} < 2$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:effk}). The \emph{indirect} channel: answer-coupled constraints are nearly all co-satisfiable, collapsing MAX-SAT to weighted majority voting (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}). The bias ratio $\text{BR} = P(\text{support} \mid \text{wrong}) / P(\text{support} \mid \text{correct})$ quantifies mirage intensity; $\text{BR} > 1$ indicates that symbolic structure amplifies rather than corrects model errors.

+The hypothesis generates three testable predictions: (1)~BR should consistently exceed 1.0 across architectures (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}); (2)~no same-model intervention---prompt-level or method-level---should reduce BR below 1.0 (\S\ref{sec:remediation}); and (3)~only verification from \emph{outside} the model's distribution can escape the mirage (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over chain-of-thought traces saturates as sample count grows because same-model traces are correlated voters.
We investigate whether symbolic constraint extraction can break this plateau through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts first-order logic (FOL) constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT.
Evaluating six models (7B--32B) across three reasoning domains with over 3,000 condition-evaluations (${\sim}$1,250 unique instances), we find that self-extracted constraints fail to surpass majority voting: none of fifteen non-degenerate conditions shows a significant positive effect ($p < 0.05$), while two conditions show significant degradation.
We identify \emph{symbolic confirmation bias} as the root cause: on incorrect problems, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC.
Process-level analysis reveals a deeper bottleneck: chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level Fleiss' $\kappa$ ($0.41$), indicating that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on answers.
Twenty-plus same-model remediation strategies spanning fifteen families all fail, revealing a persistent independence-accuracy trade-off at the 7B--32B scale: methods that increase trace independence destroy accuracy (Debate: $\kappa = 0.15$, $-18.6$\,pp), while methods preserving accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three model families).
Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound ($+29.90$\,pp and $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp ProofWriter; $p < 0.001$); same-model self-extraction captures only ${\sim}$12\% of the oracle ceiling.
However, a cross-architecture proof-of-concept---DeBERTa-large NLI combined with SC---achieves $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.039$, McNemar exact test) through per-label complementarity, demonstrating that the oracle gap is practically recoverable when verification signal comes from outside the reasoning model's distribution.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
A natural extension is to extract \emph{symbolic constraints} from reasoning traces and use formal verification to select answers---a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model or data.
We show this extension fails, and we identify why.

We name this phenomenon the \textbf{Symbolic Mirage}: self-extracted symbolic structures from an LLM are not independent verification signals but high-dimensional projections of the model's own distributional biases.
The mirage creates an illusion of formal rigor---constraints have the syntax of first-order logic and pass Z3 satisfiability checks---but their content systematically confirms the model's existing answer distribution rather than independently verifying it.

We formalize and test this hypothesis through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 condition-evaluations (${\sim}$1,250 unique instances) with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
Every experiment confirms the mirage: none of fifteen non-degenerate conditions shows a significant positive effect, and twenty-plus remediation strategies spanning fifteen families all fail (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

The evidence for the Symbolic Mirage is multi-layered.
At the answer level, Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions compresses Effective-$K$ to 1.20--3.62 for nominal $K = 12$ (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
At the constraint level, when the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
At the process level, CoT cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound ($+29.90$\,pp on FOLIO, $p < 0.001$); the mirage is the sole bottleneck, with self-extraction capturing only ${\sim}$12\% of the oracle ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
A cross-architecture proof-of-concept---DeBERTa-large NLI combined with SC---achieves $+3.43$\,pp ($p = 0.039$) by escaping the mirage entirely (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{The Symbolic Mirage Hypothesis.} We formalize the claim that self-extracted symbolic constraints are distributional projections, not independent verification (Eq.~\ref{eq:mirage}), and derive testable predictions linking bias ratio, $K_{\text{eff}}$ collapse, and aggregation degeneration (\S\ref{sec:mirage}).

\item \textbf{Quantification across architectures.} Bias ratios of $4.97\times$ (Mistral), $3.93\times$ (Qwen), and $2.88\times$ (LLaMA) confirm the mirage is universal, not model-specific. On incorrect problems, 94\% of SICA errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-level evidence.} Across four model families, CoT cosine similarity ($0.69$--$0.79$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.45$--$0.74$); the gap intensifies with capability, showing the mirage operates below the surface of answer diversity (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).

\item \textbf{Inescapability within the same model.} Twenty-plus strategies spanning fifteen families fail. The independence-accuracy trade-off ($\kappa \geq 0.40$ across three families) defines a same-model ceiling (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

\item \textbf{Cross-architecture escape.} DeBERTa-large NLI ($+3.43$\,pp, $p = 0.039$) demonstrates that verification from outside the model's distribution recovers the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}).
\end{enumerate}
